textbookText: Algae are classified into different classes on the basis of photosynthetic pigments, storage material, thallus structure and method of reproduction. It is believed that red and brown algae evolved on a different pattern and green algae are the ones that gave rise to ancestors of land plants. Here features of three classes have been described:

Green algae or chlorophyta (Greek: Chloros-green, phyton-plant) are cosmopolitan in distribution and occur in diverse habitats. They resemble land plants in their photosynthetic pigments and reserve food.

The general characters of green algae are as follows: a. Mostly they are fresh water and some grow on moist soil, wall and rocks. b. The plant body is unicellular or multicellular. c. Cell wall is made up of cellulose and pectin. d. Photosynthetic pigments are chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenes and xanthophyll. e. Reserve food material is starch. f. Reproduction takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual method.
Example: Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Chara, Chlamydomonas, Volvox, etc.

Red algae or rhodophyta (Greek: rhodon-rose, phyton-plant) are one of the oldest groups of eukaryotic algae commonly found in marine water. The red colour of rhodophyceae is due to presence of phycoerythrin.
The general characters of red algae are as follows:

a. Mostly they are marine while a few are fresh water species. b. The plant body is unicellular, filamentous, parenchymatous or ribbon like. c. Cell wall is made up of cellulose, pectin and agar. d. Photosynthetic pigments are chlorophyll a, chlorophyll d, carotenoids and phycoerythrin. e. Reserve food material is floridean starch (similar to glycogen). f. Reproduction takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual method.
Fig: 2.4.2 Different types of red algae

Brown algae or phaeophyta (Greek: phaios-dusky, dark, brown; phyta-plant) are named due to their colour, which varies from brown to olive green. The brown colour of algae is due to the presence of large amount of fucoxanthin.

The general characters of brown algae are: a. They are mostly marine. b. The plant body is branched filamentous in lower form and parenchymatous structure in higher forms. c. The cell wall is made up of cellulose, pectin and alginic acid. d. Photosynthetic pigments are chlorophyll a, chlorophyll c, carotenoids and fucoxanthin e. Reserve food material is laminarian starch and mannitol. f. Reproduction takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual method. Example: Alaria, Fucus, Laminaria, etc.
